main_ideas:1.reasoning: Defoe builds the entire passage on a single contrast: a sermon is just "a sound of words spoken to the ear" that lasts only as long as a listener's memory, while "a book printed is a record" that "conveys its contents for ages to come, to the eternity of mortal time, when the author is forgotten in his grave." The whole text is doing one job — arguing that print outlasts speech. The correct choice has to capture exactly that comparison: written words have greater permanence than spoken ones.
main_ideas:1.distractors: Reversing the comparison so that spoken messages are remembered better contradicts the passage. Limiting the claim to delivery style or to authors' personal fame narrows the idea to just one element of the contrast and ignores the central point about print outlasting speech.

main_ideas:2.reasoning: The passage uses one specific novel — The Far Side of the World — as evidence for a broader claim about the entire Aubrey/Maturin series. It notes that the abrupt ending of The Far Side of the World is only a problem if the books are read as separate texts and concludes that "the Aubrey/Maturin series is best thought of as a single incredibly long work." The main idea must therefore be a generalization about the series as a whole: each novel's structure indicates that the series should be treated as one continuous story rather than as twenty discrete books.
main_ideas:2.distractors: Choices that compare the series unfairly to The Forsyte Saga, single out two novels as especially complex, or talk about reader enjoyment despite flaws all introduce ideas the passage never argues.

main_ideas:3.reasoning: The passage explicitly sets up two camps: "Some critics have found fault with the abrupt endings" while "Other critics, however, argue that the books should not be thought of as discrete texts." The whole text is a balanced presentation of a critical disagreement about how the structure of the Aubrey/Maturin novels should be evaluated. The main idea must therefore be that critics hold differing views about the effectiveness of those structures, not that one side is right or that some specific structural feature is unusually intricate.
main_ideas:3.distractors: Picking only one of the two camps' positions, or claiming that critics want the series to imitate The Forsyte Saga, misrepresents the text by collapsing the disagreement into a single view.

main_ideas:4.reasoning: The passage opens by noting which animals were known to see in 3D and that cuttlefish were assumed not to. It then introduces Trevor Wardell's team, who "wanted to test whether this assumption was true," and reports that cuttlefish reacted to 3D images of shrimp. Every sentence is building toward overturning the prior assumption about cuttlefish vision. The main idea must be that, contrary to what researchers had thought, cuttlefish may actually possess 3D vision.
main_ideas:4.distractors: Stating only that horses and barn owls have 3D vision, or that cuttlefish resemble octopuses, focuses on background context and ignores the experiment that drives the passage.

main_ideas:5.reasoning: The text first describes Protas and colleagues, who studied convergent evolution through shared genetic mechanisms, and then Zwaan and colleagues, who studied convergence through different genetic mechanisms. Crucially, the passage says "the relative prevalence of convergence through shared and different genetic processes is still poorly understood," which is why Green and Extavour set out "to evaluate both types of convergence in a single study." The main idea is that Green and Extavour's study covers convergent evolution more comprehensively than the earlier studies, each of which examined only one mechanism.
main_ideas:5.distractors: Claims that prior researchers assumed only one mechanism was possible, or that Green and Extavour reused others' data, or that two of the studies compared both mechanisms, all add information the passage does not provide.

main_ideas:6.reasoning: Every clause about Robert is positive and points to the same conclusion: he was "daring, without being rash; prompt, but not thoughtless; firm without being harsh," and was "kind and devoted to the company he drilled," earning "the respect of his superior officers." The narrator is showing, trait by trait, that Robert has exactly the qualities a soldier needs. The main idea is therefore that Robert is well-suited to his military role.
main_ideas:6.distractors: Suggesting Robert tries hard to gain attention, that he ignores his superiors, or that he is flawed misreads the balanced, complimentary tone of the description.

main_ideas:7.reasoning: The passage starts by saying "For a long time, people thought tool use was unique to primates," and then offers a string of counter-examples — octopuses using seashells, parrots using date pits — that have "busted the myth." Every detail in the passage is evidence against the idea that only primates use tools. The main idea is that, contrary to that long-held belief, primates are not the only animals that use tools.
main_ideas:7.distractors: Singling out octopuses as exceptionally skillful, generalizing that there are many tool-use myths, or claiming that tool use is hard for animals all overstate or distort what the passage actually argues.

main_ideas:8.reasoning: The narrator describes walking through the countryside, "drinking in the air," and immediately becoming "forgetful of musty papers, of the offices, of my chief, my colleagues, my documents." In the same breath he turns to "thinking of the good things that were sure to come to me" and to memories of youth. The natural setting is doing two linked things at once: pulling his mind away from work and pushing it toward optimistic thoughts about the future and the past. The main idea has to capture both effects.
main_ideas:8.distractors: Choices that say he has quit his job, that he is strategising about his career, or that the smells distract him from urgent work all narrow or contradict the passage's actual point.

main_ideas:9.reasoning: The passage opens with Tanya Tagaq, whose work "combin[es] traditional Inuit stories with popular genres of literature." The pivotal sentence then says "Tagaq is not the only Indigenous writer" doing this and offers Stephen Graham Jones blending Blackfeet oral tradition with horror as a parallel example. The whole point is that this hybrid practice is a wider phenomenon among Indigenous writers, not the work of one author. The main idea must capture that pattern across multiple writers.
main_ideas:9.distractors: Statements about non-Indigenous authors' choices, sales figures, or the relative success of one writer add ideas the passage never advances.

main_ideas:10.reasoning: The passage explicitly contrasts two groups of Villasana's works — "In some works, Villasana focuses on celebrating cultural icons who are people of color" and "in other works, Villasana honors ordinary people" — and then unites them with the line "Villasana sees both of these approaches as ways of depicting the power and interconnectedness of all people." The main idea must capture that her art recognises both famous figures and everyday people, centring strength and connection across the two categories.
main_ideas:10.distractors: Saying that the everyday painting outweighs the famous-person paintings, that her career changed direction, or that one painting receives more scholarly attention each narrows the passage to a single example and ignores the explicit claim that her work celebrates BOTH groups.

main_ideas:11.reasoning: The passage explains what horizontal gene transfer is, notes that it can increase antibiotic resistance, and then ends by saying that "an understanding of how to prevent horizontal gene transfer might result in the mitigation of dangerous pathogens." The whole text is leading toward the practical payoff: studying this process could yield results that help people. The main idea must capture the usefulness of further study, not a particular new finding or a misconception being corrected.
main_ideas:11.distractors: Claims that a common perception is wrong, that the process is more common than was thought, or that new research is overturning earlier findings all introduce ideas the passage never raises.

main_ideas:12.reasoning: The passage points out that Lönnstedt's 2013 conclusions about ocean acidification were based on "a mean sample size of only about 28 fish," and then introduces Clements's 2022 review, which is clearly framed as scrutinizing those earlier conclusions. The text is doing one thing: signalling a possible weakness in Lönnstedt's study. The main topic must therefore be a possible shortcoming of that Pomacentrus amboinensis study, not an evolutionary discovery or a new cause of acidification.

main_ideas:13.reasoning: The passage describes a large community-science study and reports two findings: butterfly color may matter more than size, and butterflies feed more often in the morning. Both findings are about how color and time of day influence behaviour. The main idea must be the broad takeaway that a large study suggested both color and time of day might shape certain butterflies' behaviour.
main_ideas:13.distractors: Saying that location matters more, or that color matters less than time of day, contradicts the findings as stated; claiming the value of community science generally drifts away from the study's actual conclusions.

main_ideas:14.reasoning: The passage opens by saying Nixon "is most famous for his participation in the 1970s Watergate political scandal" but immediately pivots: "But Nixon's legacy is complex," listing his role in tribal-sovereignty affirmation and his attempt at health-care reform. The text uses Watergate as the well-known cloud and then highlights less-famous achievements that complicate it. The main idea has to capture the contrast: Nixon is linked with an infamous event, yet that event overshadows other notable achievements.

main_ideas:15.reasoning: The passage gives two parallel histories: "tomato" came from Nahuatl through Spanish into English, and "maize" came from Taíno through Spanish into English. The defining sentence is the opening one — "Tomato is an example of a loanword" — and the rest of the text simply offers two examples. The main idea must be the shared point: both English words are loanwords with Indigenous origins.
main_ideas:15.distractors: Claims that English supplied the words to Spanish, that Nahuatl and Taíno contributed equally, or that the meanings shifted significantly all add information the passage never provides.

main_ideas:16.reasoning: The passage frames Smith's invisible-hand metaphor as overrated: he "deploys this metaphor only once" and "to make a narrow point," and "it was largely ignored" until twentieth-century economists "eager to secure an intellectual pedigree for their views elevated it to a fully-fledged paradigm." The argument is that the fame of the metaphor comes not from its role in Smith's work but from later economists who promoted it for their own purposes. The main idea must reflect that origin of the metaphor's reputation.
main_ideas:16.distractors: Choices that endorse the metaphor as a valid model, treat it as a critique of mercantilism that anticipated later economists, or claim the metaphor turned out to be robust all soften or reverse the passage's clear scepticism.

main_ideas:17.reasoning: The passage describes McLendon's painting as "typical of paintings by the Florida Highwaymen," praises the group for "anticipating and amplifying cultural perceptions of Florida that became pervasive in the public consciousness," and notes that the imagery — placid rivers, windswept palms — was "perpetually revisited." The main idea must therefore be that the recurring images in the Highwaymen's paintings became widely associated with Florida partly because of the group's own influence.
main_ideas:17.distractors: Singling out Moonlit St. Lucie as more highly regarded than other Highwaymen works, or claiming the group's popularity declined, or that McLendon's paintings stand apart from his peers all contradict or shrink the passage's actual claim.

main_ideas:18.reasoning: The narrator describes Harris's anecdotes about a rough Channel crossing in which the well party shrinks in each retelling: first "he and the captain," then "he and the second mate," then "he and one other man," and finally "he by himself." The pattern is comic: the cast of un-seasick people changes, but Harris's own immunity to seasickness is constant. The main idea must be that Harris keeps shifting the details of his story while always boasting about his own wellness.

main_ideas:19.reasoning: The passage opens by saying Barragán's career "evolved through distinct phases" and then traces a specific change: after travelling to the United States and Europe in the early 1930s, he began "incorporating principles derived from functionalism and modernism." The contrast between his earlier historically inspired houses and the later geometric church is offered as evidence of that shift. The main idea must therefore highlight the change in his design aesthetic and tie it to his time abroad.

main_ideas:20.reasoning: The passage's structure is a single "Like X… However, because X is highly specialized, it is especially vulnerable" construction. It first describes the Kaua'i 'amakihi as adapted to a narrow Hawaiian habitat with specialized traits, and then warns that this same specialization makes it "especially vulnerable to environmental changes." The main idea must combine both halves: the bird is unique to Hawaii, highly specialized, and therefore particularly susceptible to disturbance.

main_ideas:21.reasoning: Padre Florentino is alone by the sea, "relieving the monotony by playing on his harmonium sad and melancholy tunes." The passage explicitly links the music to his mood: it is sad because he is sad. The main idea must capture that connection — the sadness of his playing reflects his own feelings.
main_ideas:21.distractors: Statements about the residence's isolation, his preference for playing over listening, or his ambition to be a skilled musician all elevate background details into themes the passage does not pursue.

main_ideas:22.reasoning: Emerson calls scholars "priests of that thought which establishes the foundations of the earth" and warns that it is "a common calamity if they neglect their post in a country where the material interest is so predominant as it is in America." The argument is that in a society obsessed with material things, scholars must keep ideas alive. The main idea must capture that role — the urgency of cultivating ideas in a materialistic country.

main_ideas:23.reasoning: The passage gives The Fifty-Year Mission credit — "clearly a unique and valuable resource" — but then identifies "a shortcoming common among oral histories: it lacks a clear authorial point of view that could otherwise unite the various accounts into a cohesive whole." Both the praise and the criticism must be reflected. The main idea is that the work is a worthwhile, comprehensive effort with one important limitation built into its approach.

main_ideas:24.reasoning: The passage opens with a question — why do black-footed cats purr but leopards roar? — and then proposes that the answer "may be partly due to a U-shaped bone in their throats called the hyoid." Each subsequent sentence describes how the hyoid differs between the two species and how those differences allow purring vs. roaring. The main idea must therefore link the hyoid differences to the explanation for the purring-versus-roaring contrast.

main_ideas:25.reasoning: The passage reports a finding from van Berlo et al. — players don't recall product information well from advergames — and then says "This phenomenon can be explained by" Lang's limited-capacity model. The whole passage is doing one thing: using Lang's model to explain van Berlo's finding. The main idea must reflect that Lang's model provides a means of explaining the van Berlo result.
main_ideas:25.distractors: Choices that claim van Berlo measured purchasing behaviour, that Lang's model contradicts the result, or that the two studies independently reach the same conclusion misstate the relationship the passage actually draws.

main_ideas:26.reasoning: Like the Kaua'i 'amakihi passage, this one builds on a "specialised therefore vulnerable" structure. It introduces the 'akeke'e as adapted to a narrow Hawaiian habitat with specialised traits, then warns that the very specialization makes it "especially vulnerable to environmental changes." The main idea must capture both halves: the bird is unique to Hawaii, highly specialised, and therefore particularly susceptible to habitat disturbance.

main_ideas:27.reasoning: The passage gives community science two explicit benefits: it "can promote community engagement by offering insight into the daily life of a scientist" and it "greatly increases the amount of data that can be collected." The Herzel butterfly study is offered as an example of both. The main idea must combine both benefits — increased public understanding of scientists' work and substantially more data — pointing to community science as good for communities and for researchers.

main_ideas:28.reasoning: The passage opens with the situation it wants to discuss — "an animal will encounter another member of its own species that it doesn't have any connection with" — and then poses several questions that flow from that scenario. Every sentence is anchored to that one type of meeting. The main topic must therefore be precisely that: a kind of meeting between animals of the same species.

main_ideas:29.reasoning: Defoe again contrasts spoken and printed words. The sermon is "a sound of words spoken to the ear," which lasts only as long as the listener can remember it; a printed book is "a record, remaining in every man's possession," always available to renew its acquaintance with memory. The whole passage is a single comparison driving toward one claim: print outlives speech. The main idea must capture that greater permanence of print over spoken words.

main_ideas:30.reasoning: The passage reports that more Quito residents than Buenos Aires residents use parks (82.9% vs 69.9%) but then stresses that "the percentage of Quito respondents who reported having access to other desired amenities near parks was much lower than that reported by Buenos Aires respondents," so amenities cannot explain the difference. The main idea must say both things: there is a gap in park use, and that gap is not due to greater access to nearby amenities in Quito.

main_ideas:31.reasoning: The narrator stands inside her newly rented apartment and reflects that her destiny has "delivered me unexpected moments," sometimes catching her ready and sometimes not. The reflection only makes sense if THIS moment — moving into the apartment — is one of those turning points. The main idea must capture the narrator's recognition that this particular moment marks a major shift in her life.

main_ideas:32.reasoning: The passage sets up a tension: critics warned that writing in Gikuyu "might make his works inaccessible outside his own community," yet "Ngugi went on to author dozens of acclaimed works in Gikuyu that have been translated into a total of more than thirty languages." The main idea must yoke both halves together: scepticism on one side, but literary success on the other.

main_ideas:33.reasoning: The narrator stands at the bow watching the urban landscape "disappearing behind us" and then perceives the viaduct of Point du Jour as the boundary between the city and the countryside. The river itself changes character in step with the landscape. The main idea must capture that parallel: the shift from urban to rural environment is mirrored in the river's own changes.

main_ideas:34.reasoning: The fuller passage says explicitly that beyond the Point du Jour the Seine is "suddenly spreading out as though it had regained space and liberty" and "became all at once the peaceful river which flows through the plains." The implicit comparison is to the river inside Paris, which is bounded and rougher. The main idea must therefore say that the Seine is more confined and rough in Paris than in the countryside.

main_ideas:35.reasoning: The passage opens by acknowledging that the sonnet has "strict formal requirements" and yet showcases two very different examples. It then quotes Carl Phillips: "the form invites experimentation" precisely because its conventions are so recognizable. The main idea is that the sonnet, despite seeming rigid, encourages a surprising amount of variety.

main_ideas:36.reasoning: The Givon team trained goldfish to drive a motorised tank on land toward a pink board, and the fish succeeded often enough that the team concluded the fish's "navigational skills aren't specific to an aquatic environment." The whole passage is one experiment driving one conclusion. The main idea must be that, with mechanical help, fish can navigate even on land.

main_ideas:37.reasoning: The passage opens by saying "Women like Dorothy T. Blum made important early contributions to the history of US cryptology," and then describes Blum's NSA work. It explicitly notes that her efforts "helped make it possible for more women — such as Maureen Baginski" — to follow. The whole passage is about women's contributions, with Blum and Baginski as examples. The main idea must reflect that broader topic, not a niche claim about cryptology or the two women collaborating.

main_ideas:38.reasoning: The passage situates Drelichman and Voth's work within other research on European early modern state finance, then highlights their "unique contribution": reconstructing the earliest extant set of annual fiscal records, which lets them show that Philip II's defaults were caused by short-term cash shortages rather than unsustainable debts. The main idea must capture the joint point — they advanced the field by assembling new evidence that yielded a specific insight into Philip II's defaults.
